description: Honestly, there aren’t really any specific requirements. If you know how to use AI tools and can build stuff with them, you’re in. If you know design and can make things look good, you’re in too. You don’t need to be an expert or know everything. Just bring whatever you’re good at, and we’ll figure out the rest together.
summary: So, What is firelens it is an platform that organized the scatter data of NASA. The data is gold mine, but it is so scatter that it can't be use so, Firelen give access that whole data with AI assistance to an simple user or engineer who want to learn about the NASA datasets and have some question he can ask the ai assistance. The AI assistance don't assume anything it gets the official data.
details:
Flame in Freefall is an evidence workbench for NASA's microgravity combustion research. It answers one question honestly: what can NASA's combustion archive actually support about fire safety in a spacecraft cabin, a lunar habitat, and a Mars base?

The interface is built on a dated snapshot of the NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository: 24 Combustion Science investigations, 22 experimental summary tables normalized into 2,870 test rows, 109 report and science-document records, and 352 publications. Raw instrument files (65,629 entries, petabytes) are indexed as metadata but never downloaded.

The flagship view is an Oxygen × Gravity Evidence Map. Every tabulated test condition is plotted by reported oxygen concentration against gravity environment, with solid, liquid, and gaseous fuels separated. A shaded band marks the ≥30% O₂ lunar habitat target. The partial-gravity lane is deliberately empty and annotated as such. The headline finding is an absence, not a number: zero direct partial-gravity combustion datasets exist in this snapshot. The nearest solid-material evidence peaks at 22.2% O₂ (BASS-II); the eight table points that reach ≥30% O₂ are all gaseous or droplet experiments.

Around that sit an investigation explorer (all 24 records filterable by gravity class, material phase, and data availability), per-record pages with normalized conditions and provenance, and a grounded evidence assistant.

How it works

Two Python ingestion scripts rebuild everything from the public PSI API. build_dataset.py reads the investigation records, experimental-table CSVs, and file trees, and normalizes them into static JSON with strict rules: missing values stay null, malformed oxygen strings are excluded rather than corrected, only initial/ambient test conditions are used, and every number keeps a link back to its source table, row, and column. fetch_documents.py downloads the Reports and Science Documents of every investigation through the public PSI file API, extracts text page by page, and splits it into 2,583 overlapping page-stamped passages from 91 documents.

Every assistant question is ranked against that corpus with Okapi BM25 — a lexical ranker with no model, no API key, and no vector database, so it behaves identically on a free hosting tier and on a laptop. Matching passages are shown to the reader verbatim with their document title and page number. If a language model is available it may only use the retrieved context, and its draft is accepted only if every percentage it mentions appears in the normalized tables or in a cited passage; otherwise the draft is rejected and the deterministic answer is served with a note explaining why. With no API key at all, the assistant still answers from the tables and the report corpus.

Benefits and intended impact

Fire-safety engineers sizing a materials envelope before a design review get a citable answer with provenance instead of a summary of a summary. Mission designers get an explicit comparison: the spacecraft-cabin scenario rests on direct microgravity evidence; the lunar and Mars scenarios are analogical plus gap, and the interface says so before it shows a number. The value is in what the workbench refuses to claim — it prevents an unsupported lunar fire-safety claim from being made on the strength of a microgravity result. Everything is reproducible: re-run the scripts and the site rebuilds itself.

Tools

Next.js 16 (App Router, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4), Python 3.14 with pypdf and python-docx for ingestion, a read-only FastAPI mirror of the snapshot, Lucide icons, IBM Plex Sans/Mono, and the Groq API for the optional model lane. Deployed on Vercel and GitHub Pages. No proprietary datasets, no paywalled services, and no vector database.

Creativity

Three ideas shape it. First, the subject is an absence, and the interface is designed to make absence legible rather than to fill it — the empty lane, four explicit evidence classes, and a page of known limits. Second, the retrieval layer is deliberately simple: BM25 over verbatim NASA text, with page-level citations, means no hallucinated numbers can enter the answers and no embedding service is needed. Third, the numeric guard extends a table-level check into free-text answers: a percentage is acceptable only if it exists in the normalized tables or in the passage being cited. The hero is an isometric combustion bench, drawn as a real instrument in which turning the gravity knob morphs the flame from a 1 g teardrop into a free sphere — the premise of the project rendered as one object a reader can operate.

Factors the team considered

Data honesty came first: we built the snapshot before the interface, wrote the normalization rules before the charts, and refused to estimate any missing value. We treated not reported, zero, and no evidence as three different states throughout. We kept the assistant optional and the deterministic path always working, so the tool never depends on a model being online. We built for the smallest screens and for logged-out judges. We considered a hosted RAG endpoint and a vector database and chose against both, because a lexical index over 91 real NASA documents is auditable, reproducible, and free. And we kept the scope honest: this is a snapshot, not a live PSI mirror, and every claim states that.
